title: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection
goal: By the end you can predict where every task in a burst goes (a core thread, the queue, an extra thread, or the rejection handler) and configure a ThreadPoolExecutor that pushes back instead of growing without limit.

warmup.q: `new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 10, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>())` gets a burst of 50 tasks that each take 2 seconds. What is the most threads it will run at once?
warmup.why: The pool only adds threads beyond core when the queue refuses a task. A `LinkedBlockingQueue` with no capacity never refuses, so the pool stays at 2 threads and 48 tasks wait in the queue. `maximumPoolSize` never comes into play.

sections.h: Four rules decide where every task goes
sections.body:
`Executors.newFixedThreadPool`, `newCachedThreadPool` and `newSingleThreadExecutor` are all built on one class, `ThreadPoolExecutor`. Its main constructor takes five settings:

```java
new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    2,                              // corePoolSize
    4,                              // maximumPoolSize
    60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,           // keepAliveTime for threads above core
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2),    // the work queue
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());  // what to do when everything is full
```

```kotlin
ThreadPoolExecutor(
    2,                                  // corePoolSize
    4,                                  // maximumPoolSize
    60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,               // keepAliveTime for threads above core
    ArrayBlockingQueue(2),              // the work queue
    ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy())   // what to do when everything is full
```

Every call to `execute` walks the same four rules, in this order:

1. Fewer than `corePoolSize` threads? Start a new thread for this task, even if other threads are idle.
2. Otherwise, offer the task to the queue.
3. The queue said no? Start a new thread, if that stays within `maximumPoolSize`.
4. Still no room? Hand the task to the `RejectedExecutionHandler`.

Read rule 3 again, because it surprises almost everyone. The pool grows past core only when the queue is full. Most people expect the opposite: use more threads first, queue when you run out. `ThreadPoolExecutor` prefers queuing because it keeps the thread count small. Extra threads are a relief valve for bursts, not the main capacity.

Here is that pool taking seven 500 ms tasks, from `PoolPuzzleDemo`:

```text
task 1 accepted: threads=1 queued=0
task 2 accepted: threads=2 queued=0
task 3 accepted: threads=2 queued=1
task 4 accepted: threads=2 queued=2
task 5 accepted: threads=3 queued=2
task 6 accepted: threads=4 queued=2
task 7 REJECTED: threads=4 queued=2
```

Tasks 1 and 2 start core threads. Tasks 3 and 4 wait. Tasks 5 and 6 find the queue full and get extra threads. Task 7 finds everything full and is rejected with `RejectedExecutionException`.

One more detail: tasks 5 and 6 run before tasks 3 and 4. A new thread takes the task that made it, not the oldest task in the queue. Even a pool with a first-in, first-out queue does not promise first-in, first-out execution.

sections.h: An unbounded queue turns maximumPoolSize into dead code
sections.body:
`Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)` is `new ThreadPoolExecutor(n, n, 0, MILLISECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>())`. The queue has no capacity limit, so rule 2 always succeeds. Rule 3 never runs, so no extra thread is ever started, and rule 4 never runs either, so nothing is ever rejected.

That sounds safe. It isn't. An unbounded queue hides overload instead of reporting it. Say your authorization service gets 400 requests a second and the pool can finish 300. The queue grows by 100 tasks every second. After ten minutes, 60,000 tasks are waiting, each holding its request in memory, and a new request waits more than three minutes before a thread even looks at it. The client gave up long ago, so the pool is now doing work nobody wants. The first alert you get is probably the heap.

Setting a larger `maximumPoolSize` on such a pool changes nothing. `new ThreadPoolExecutor(10, 100, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>())` runs 10 threads, forever. The `100` is dead code.

`newCachedThreadPool()` fails the other way. It is `new ThreadPoolExecutor(0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, 60, SECONDS, new SynchronousQueue<>())`. A `SynchronousQueue` has no capacity at all: an offer succeeds only if an idle thread is waiting to take it. Under a burst no thread is idle, so every task gets a new thread. Two thousand slow calls means two thousand threads.

There is one shape that pushes back: a **bounded queue with a finite maximum**. Then rule 4 can fire, and overload turns into a visible event that you choose how to handle. The sizes come from lesson 3 of this track. The shape comes from this one.

One edge case is worth knowing. With `corePoolSize` 0 and an unbounded queue, rule 1 never starts a thread and rule 3 never runs, so it looks as if nothing would ever execute. The pool special-cases this: after queuing, if it has no threads at all, it starts one. You get a single-threaded pool.

try.title: Swap the queue
steps: Predict the thread count and total time for the same seven tasks with an unbounded queue. Then run the demo with `-Pargs=unbounded`.
Do the same with `-Pargs=handoff`, which uses a `SynchronousQueue`.
try.expect: With `unbounded`, the pool never goes past 2 threads, all seven tasks are accepted, five of them queue, and the run takes about 2,000 ms (four rounds of 500 ms). With `handoff`, nothing ever queues: tasks 1 to 4 each get a thread and tasks 5, 6 and 7 are rejected, because max is 4 and a `SynchronousQueue` holds nothing.

sections.h: Rejection policies decide who pays when the pool is full
sections.body:
When rule 4 fires, the pool calls its `RejectedExecutionHandler`. The same handler runs for any task submitted after `shutdown()`. The JDK ships four:

| Policy | What happens to the task | Who notices |
|---|---|---|
| `AbortPolicy` (the default) | `execute` throws `RejectedExecutionException` | the caller, at once |
| `CallerRunsPolicy` | the submitting thread runs it itself | the caller, by being slowed down |
| `DiscardPolicy` | dropped | nobody |
| `DiscardOldestPolicy` | the oldest queued task is dropped, then the new one is retried | nobody |

`AbortPolicy` is the right default for request handling. The caller gets an exception it can turn into an HTTP 503 or a retry, and you can count it.

`CallerRunsPolicy` is **back-pressure** in one line. While the submitting thread is busy running a task, it isn't submitting more, so the producer slows to the pool's speed. It suits a batch job that reads files and fans out work. It is a bad idea when the caller is a thread that must never block: an event-loop thread (one thread that serves many connections, so it must never wait on any one of them), or a Kafka consumer thread that has to call `poll()` again within `max.poll.interval.ms`. After `shutdown()` it drops the task silently.

The two discard policies lose work without a trace. They have a nastier side with `submit`. A dropped `FutureTask` never runs, so its `Future` never completes, and a caller blocked in `get()` waits forever. Use them only for work that is truly optional, like a best-effort metrics flush.

In production you usually want a custom handler: count the rejection for a metric, then fail fast with a message that says how full the pool was. The interface has one method, `rejectedExecution(Runnable task, ThreadPoolExecutor pool)`, and the lab has you write it.

try.title: Try the other three policies
steps: Run the demo with `-Pargs="bounded caller"`. Find the line for task 7. Which thread ran it, and when was the `accepted` line printed?
Run it with `-Pargs="bounded discard"` and then `-Pargs="bounded oldest"`. Count the `done` lines and work out which task disappeared each time.
try.expect: With `caller`, task 7 runs on `main`, so `main` is stuck for 500 ms and prints "task 7 accepted" only after `task 7 done on main`. With `discard`, task 7 is "accepted" and simply never runs: six `done` lines, no error. With `oldest`, task 3 (the oldest queued task) vanishes and task 7 runs instead. Neither discard policy says a word about it.

sections.h: Keep-alive, core time-out and prestarting threads
sections.body:
Threads above `corePoolSize` are temporary. If one sits idle for longer than `keepAliveTime`, it exits and the pool shrinks back toward core. Core threads stay, even if they are idle for a week.

Two methods change that default.

`allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true)` applies the keep-alive to core threads as well, so an idle pool can shrink to zero threads. That suits a pool used for a nightly report: it holds no threads for the rest of the day. It needs a keep-alive greater than zero, or the call throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

`prestartAllCoreThreads()` goes the other way. By default even core threads are created lazily, one per task, the first time tasks arrive. Prestarting creates them all up front, so the first burst after a deploy doesn't also pay for thread creation. The Javadoc also recommends it when you build a pool around a queue that already holds tasks, since a pool with no threads would never look at them.

You can watch the whole lifecycle with the getters: `getPoolSize()` (threads alive now), `getActiveCount()` (threads running a task), `getLargestPoolSize()` (the high-water mark) and `getQueue().size()`. They are approximate while the pool is busy, which is fine for dashboards. Lesson 9 of this track turns them into metrics.

For most request-handling pools I set core equal to max and rely on a bounded queue plus a rejection policy. A pool whose size changes under load is harder to reason about, and the extra threads arrive exactly when the machine is busiest. Keep core below max when bursts are short and rare, and you would rather absorb them than reject.

try.expect: The pool starts with 0 threads, jumps to 4 during the burst, and drops back to 2 a few hundred milliseconds after the work ends. The largest pool size reported is 4. With `core`, it drops from 4 to 2 and then to 0, because the core threads now retire too.

analogy: A `ThreadPoolExecutor` is a restaurant. The core threads are the permanent waiters. The queue is the waiting area by the door. Maximum pool size is how many temporary staff the manager may call in, and the manager calls them only when the waiting area is full, never just because the waiters look busy. The rejection policy is the door policy when the waiting area is packed and every temp is working: turn guests away (`AbortPolicy`), make the person at the door serve them himself (`CallerRunsPolicy`), or quietly lose a booking (the discard policies). The analogy breaks on fairness. A real restaurant seats people in arrival order. A new temp in this pool serves the guest who arrived last.
in_your_world: A Kafka consumer for card authorizations fans each record out to a pool so slow issuer calls don't block polling. If that pool is `newFixedThreadPool(16)`, a slow issuer quietly fills an unbounded queue while offsets march on, and a crash loses everything in it. Give it a bounded queue. Then decide what overload means. If the consumer should slow down, `CallerRunsPolicy` makes the polling thread do the work, but watch `max.poll.interval.ms` (300,000 ms by default): if one run of work on that thread takes longer than that, the consumer is removed from the group and its partitions are reassigned. If overload should fail fast, keep `AbortPolicy` with a counting handler, pause the partition, and alert on the counter. Quarkus and Temporal size their own worker pools from configuration; the same four rules apply to the ones you build.
mistake: Raising `maximumPoolSize` to fix a slow pool that uses an unbounded queue. Someone sees `newFixedThreadPool(8)` falling behind, swaps in `new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 64, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>())`, and nothing changes, because the pool only grows past core when the queue is full and this queue is never full. Either raise `corePoolSize`, or give the queue a capacity so the pool can grow and eventually reject.

compare.title: Configuring the same pool from Java and Kotlin

java.title: AuthPool.java (solution)

kotlin.title: AuthPoolConfig.kt
kotlin.src:
package workbench.executors.l02

import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue
import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong

val rejectedAuths = AtomicLong()

// Java constructors take no named arguments in Kotlin, so the comments do that job.
fun authPool(): ThreadPoolExecutor = ThreadPoolExecutor(
    4, 8,                               // core, max
    30, TimeUnit.SECONDS,               // keep-alive for threads above core
    ArrayBlockingQueue(16),             // Runnable is inferred from the parameter type
) { _, pool ->                          // RejectedExecutionHandler, written as a trailing lambda
    rejectedAuths.incrementAndGet()
    throw RejectedExecutionException("rejected: queued=${pool.queue.size}")
}.apply { prestartAllCoreThreads() }

fun main() {
    val pool = authPool()
    println("threads before any task: ${pool.poolSize}")
    pool.shutdown()
}

compare.note: The pool is the same Java object, but two things differ when you build it from Kotlin. Kotlin does not allow named arguments when calling a Java constructor, so seven positional numbers need comments in both languages. And Kotlin converts a lambda to a Java single-method interface, so the `RejectedExecutionHandler` can be a trailing lambda instead of a class. The getters read as properties (`pool.queue`, `pool.poolSize`). In coroutine code you rarely build one at all: `Dispatchers.IO` is already a shared pool capped at 64 threads (or the core count, if larger), and `limitedParallelism(n)` gives you a smaller limit on top of it.

worked.title: Trace a rebalance burst through the authorization pool

steps.say: This is the pool from the lab. After a Kafka rebalance, the consumer gets 30 authorizations at once, and each one waits about 200 ms on the issuer. Before reading on, write down how many threads start, how many tasks queue and how many are rejected.
steps.code:
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());
steps.alt_code:
val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(
    4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    ArrayBlockingQueue(16),
    ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy())

steps.say: Apply the rules in order. Tasks 1 to 4 start the core threads (rule 1). Tasks 5 to 20 fill the queue of 16 (rule 2). Tasks 21 to 24 find the queue full and start extra threads, up to 8 (rule 3). Tasks 25 to 30 find everything full and are rejected (rule 4).

Six `RejectedExecutionException`s reach the consumer. If that thread doesn't catch them, it dies, and the records are redelivered after the next rebalance, which causes the next burst. Decide on purpose instead. Here the right answer is to slow the consumer down, so the burst drains at the pool's pace.
steps.code:
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());   // the consumer thread runs overflow itself
steps.alt_code:
val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(
    4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    ArrayBlockingQueue(16),
    ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy())   // the consumer thread runs overflow itself

steps.say: Now tasks 25 to 30 run on the consumer thread, one after another: about 6 x 200 ms = 1.2 s during which the consumer can't poll. That is far below the 5 minute `max.poll.interval.ms`, so the trade is fine here. If one task could take minutes, it wouldn't be, and you would pause the partition instead.

lab.title: Predict a pool, configure a pool, handle its rejections
steps: Run the tests. All twelve fail.

Write `PoolMath.predict`. Loop over the tasks and apply the four rules to three counters. The tests compare your answers with a real `ThreadPoolExecutor` on eight configurations, including a `SynchronousQueue` (capacity 0) and an unbounded queue.
Write `AuthPool.create` to the spec in its Javadoc. Don't forget the part about starting the core threads up front.
Write `CountingRejectionHandler`: count every call, return quietly if the pool is shut down, otherwise throw `RejectedExecutionException` with the message format from the Javadoc.
Run the tests until all twelve pass.
hints: `predict` needs no special case for capacity 0 or `Integer.MAX_VALUE`. The comparison `queued < queueCapacity` already handles both.
`ThreadPoolExecutor` has a constructor that takes a `RejectedExecutionHandler` as its sixth argument. `prestartAllCoreThreads()` is a method you call after construction.
Use a `LongAdder` or `AtomicLong` for the count: several submitting threads can be rejected at the same moment.

drill.title: Run the four rules in your head
drill.prompt: Close this page. From memory, write the four rules `ThreadPoolExecutor.execute` applies, in order. Then predict threads, queued and rejected for `new ThreadPoolExecutor(3, 6, 60, SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4))` with 15 tasks that all block. Last, do the same with `new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()` as the queue.

answer.src:
1. fewer than core threads  -> start a new thread
2. otherwise                 -> offer to the queue
3. queue refused             -> start a thread if below max
4. otherwise                 -> RejectedExecutionHandler

ArrayBlockingQueue(4), 15 tasks:
  tasks 1-3   core threads      threads = 3
  tasks 4-7   queued            queued  = 4
  tasks 8-10  extra threads     threads = 6
  tasks 11-15 rejected          rejected = 5

LinkedBlockingQueue (unbounded), 15 tasks:
  threads = 3, queued = 12, rejected = 0   (max = 6 is never used)

recap: `execute` applies four rules in order: below core, start a thread; else queue; if the queue refuses, grow toward max; else reject.
The pool grows past core only when the queue is full, so with an unbounded queue `maximumPoolSize` does nothing.
`newFixedThreadPool` hides overload in an unbounded queue. `newCachedThreadPool` turns it into unbounded threads. A bounded queue with a finite max pushes back.
`AbortPolicy` throws, `CallerRunsPolicy` slows the submitter, and the two discard policies lose work silently (and leave `submit` futures that never complete).
`keepAliveTime` retires idle threads above core. `allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true)` retires core threads too. `prestartAllCoreThreads()` starts them early.

quiz.q: `new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 60, SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10))` receives 8 tasks that each block for a minute. Where are they?
quiz.why: Tasks 1 and 2 start core threads. The other 6 fit in a queue of 10, so the queue never refuses and the pool never grows. The tempting answer, 4 running, assumes the pool uses its max before queuing. It is the other way round.

quiz.q: A batch job reads 2 million ledger rows and submits one task per 1,000 rows. You want it to run no faster than the pool can keep up, without losing a batch and without a retry loop. Which handler fits?
quiz.why: `CallerRunsPolicy` makes the reading thread run the overflow batch itself, so it stops reading while it works. That is back-pressure, and nothing is lost. `AbortPolicy` would make you write the retry loop, and both discard policies lose batches without telling anyone.

quiz.q: A pool uses `DiscardPolicy`. A request thread calls `pool.submit(task).get()` while the pool is saturated. What happens?
options: `get()` blocks forever, because the dropped task never runs and its Future never completes
quiz.why: `DiscardPolicy` drops the `FutureTask` without running or cancelling it. Nothing will ever complete that `Future`, so `get()` without a timeout waits forever. This is why the Javadoc suggests cancelling dropped tasks in a custom handler.

quiz.q: A pool with core 4, max 16 and a bounded queue grew to 16 threads during a spike an hour ago. Traffic is quiet now. With default settings, how many threads does it have?
options: 4, because idle threads above core retired after keepAliveTime
quiz.why: Keep-alive applies to threads above core, so the pool shrinks back to 4. It only goes to 0 if you call `allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true)`.

quiz.q: From "Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown": a producer thread keeps calling `execute` on a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with the default handler after another thread has called `shutdown()`. What does the producer see?
options: The tasks run, because shutdown() lets queued work finish
A RejectedExecutionException from each execute call
Nothing: the tasks are silently dropped
quiz.why: After `shutdown()`, new tasks go to the rejection handler, and the default `AbortPolicy` throws `RejectedExecutionException`. Only tasks that were already queued still run. With a discard policy or `CallerRunsPolicy` they would be dropped silently instead.

flashcards.front: In what order does `ThreadPoolExecutor.execute` try its options?
flashcards.back: Start a thread if below core; else queue; if the queue refuses, start a thread if below max; else reject.

flashcards.front: Why does `newFixedThreadPool(8)` never run more than 8 threads, whatever max you set?
flashcards.back: Its `LinkedBlockingQueue` is unbounded, so the queue never refuses a task, and the pool only grows past core when the queue refuses.

flashcards.front: What queue does `newCachedThreadPool()` use, and what is the risk?
flashcards.back: A `SynchronousQueue` (no capacity) with max `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, so every task that finds no idle thread gets a new thread. Threads grow without limit.

flashcards.front: What does `CallerRunsPolicy` do with an overflow task?
flashcards.back: The thread that called `execute` runs it, which slows that producer down. After shutdown it drops the task.

flashcards.front: A pool with `DiscardPolicy` drops a task sent with `submit`. What happens to `future.get()`?
flashcards.back: It blocks forever. The task never runs, so its Future never completes.

flashcards.front: What does `keepAliveTime` apply to by default?
flashcards.back: Only to threads above `corePoolSize`. Call `allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true)` to let core threads retire too.

flashcards.front: When does a new extra thread pick up a queued task first?
flashcards.back: It doesn't. A thread started by rule 3 runs the task that triggered it, so later tasks can overtake queued ones.

terms.plain: The number of threads the pool keeps, even when idle.
The most threads the pool may run, reached only when the queue is full.
The BlockingQueue where tasks wait for a free thread.
A SynchronousQueue: no storage, a task passes straight to an idle thread or not at all.
The callback that decides what happens to a task the pool cannot take.
Slowing the producer down when the consumer can't keep up, instead of piling up work.
How long an idle thread above core waits before it exits.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate set `maximumPoolSize` to 64 on a pool built with `new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()` and says the pool "can scale to 64 threads under load". Explain why it can't, and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: A ThreadPoolExecutor only starts threads beyond core when the queue refuses a task. A LinkedBlockingQueue with no capacity never refuses, so every task past the core threads waits in the queue, and the pool never goes above corePoolSize. The 64 is never used. The queue also grows without limit when we fall behind, so we see memory growth and long waits instead of a clear overload signal. I would pick a core size from the expected load, give the queue a capacity, set max as the burst limit, and choose a rejection policy on purpose: usually AbortPolicy with a counter for request handling, or CallerRunsPolicy if the producer should slow down.

deeper.body:
Why does `ThreadPoolExecutor` queue before it grows? Its Javadoc lists three queuing strategies and is honest about each. A direct handoff (`SynchronousQueue`) "avoids lockups when handling sets of requests that might have internal dependencies", because a task never waits behind another task that it depends on, but it needs an unbounded max. An unbounded queue suits independent tasks and smooths bursts, but "admits the possibility of unbounded work queue growth". A bounded queue "helps prevent resource exhaustion" but "can be more difficult to tune": a large queue with a small pool keeps CPU use low and can give "artificially low throughput", while a small queue needs a larger pool.

That first point comes back in lesson 9 of this track as pool-induced deadlock: tasks that wait for other tasks in the same bounded pool.

Two more details for when you read pool code. First, core and max can be changed at runtime with `setCorePoolSize` and `setMaximumPoolSize`, which is how some frameworks resize pools from configuration without a restart. Second, `ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor` extends `ThreadPoolExecutor` but uses its own unbounded delay queue, so its max setting has no useful effect: it is a fixed pool of `corePoolSize` threads. Lesson 5 of this track covers it.
